notes: Service-out and forum conveniens challenge on joinder of TRNC company; United Film v Chabria governs CPR 6.20(3).

enrichment.short_title: Trumann v Societe Generale: service on CCL in TRNC
key_facts: Trumann, through Dr Sel, sued Mr and Mrs Kansu and related companies for breach of fiduciary duty in transferring assets from CCI to CCL.
CCL, a company in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, applied to set aside service out and challenge jurisdiction.
Master Moncaster had permitted joinder of CCL for tracing and accounting claims arising from alleged breaches by the Kansus.
CCL had commenced and discontinued English proceedings against Trumann, then issued parallel proceedings in TRNC shortly before the joinder hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside service out of the jurisdiction on CCL and to challenge the English court's jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; England was the proper forum and joinder of CCL was permitted under CPR 6.20(3) and (5) as construed in United Film v Chabria.
enrichment.ratio: Under United Film v Chabria, CPR 6.20(3) is equivalent in effect to CPR 19.2(2); a foreign defendant may be served out where there is a real issue with an existing party and the new party is a necessary or proper party; forum shopping by parallel TRNC proceedings did not make England an inappropriate forum.
legal_issues: Whether CCL's application to set aside was an abuse of process under Johnson v Gore Wood
Construction of CPR 6.20(3) for joinder and service out
Whether claims against CCL fell within CPR 6.20(5) on contract grounds
Whether England or TRNC was the forum conveniens
linked_authorities: United Film Distribution v Chabria [2001] 2 All ER (Comm) 865
Youell v Kara Mara Shipping [2000] 2 Lloyd's Rep 102

confidence.notes: Outcome and CPR analysis are explicit. Some factual background on corporate structure is complex but clearly stated.

notes: Oil-for-Food steel shipment dispute; repudiatory breach turns on provenance of defective d-bars on the Tiger V.

enrichment.short_title: Log-O-Mar v Craft: rogue d-bars and settlement agreement breach
key_facts: Log-O-Mar chartered vessels to Craft and Croyndon to carry steel d-bars from Jebel Ali to Umm Qasr under a November 2001 settlement agreement.
Brittle rogue 12 mm d-bars caused repeated discharge delays at Umm Qasr and the Tiger V eventually sailed back to Jebel Ali with cargo still on board.
Log-O-Mar treated the settlement as repudiated on 26 April 2002; Craft denied obligation to take delivery of remaining cargo.
Expert evidence showed samples C and D had abnormal manganese content making bundles liable to break during normal handling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for balance of voyage costs under settlement agreement and counterclaim for damages.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; rogue d-bars more likely came from the Nordsund cargo; Log-O-Mar was in repudiatory breach and not entitled to recover outstanding voyage costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where legally dangerous cargo on the Tiger V originated from the Nordsund rather than the Mega S, Log-O-Mar was not entitled to treat Craft as in repudiatory breach; payment of the balance of voyage costs was conditional on completion of discharging at Umm Qasr, unlike The Karin Vatis and The Lefthero.
legal_issues: Which party was in repudiatory breach of the settlement agreement
Whether rogue d-bars came from Mega S or Nordsund cargo
Whether Log-O-Mar could recover voyage costs after its own repudiatory breach
Construction of cost-payment clause as condition precedent

confidence.notes: Factual findings on cargo provenance and contractual construction are detailed. Some loading/discharge records were inconclusive but the judge's balance of probabilities conclusion is clear.

notes: Highway maintenance appeal; section 41 duty is repair not layout; Gorringe and Goodes applied.

enrichment.short_title: Thompson v Hampshire: ditch beside campsite path and section 41
key_facts: Ms Thompson fell into a ditch beside an unofficial footpath on the A337 verge near a New Forest campsite at night and broke her ankle.
The path and ditch were part of the highway but the council did not know of the beaten path before the accident.
The claim was solely for breach of statutory duty under section 41, not common law negligence.
The ditch and culvert were not in disrepair; the complaint was essentially about dangerous juxtaposition of path and ditch.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial judge's dismissal of claim for breach of highway authority's statutory duty to maintain.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; no breach of section 41 because the duty is to repair the fabric of the highway, not to address layout or transient vegetation.
enrichment.ratio: Following Goodes and Gorringe, section 41 imposes a duty to repair the physical surface of the highway, not a general duty to make the highway safe or to address layout; complaints about path-ditch juxtaposition and overgrown grass are matters of layout or obstruction, not disrepair, and trap arguments belong in negligence not statutory duty.
legal_issues: Scope of the section 41 duty to maintain highways
Whether path-ditch juxtaposition rendered the highway out of repair
Whether overgrown vegetation made the path out of repair
Applicability of section 66 powers versus section 41 duty
linked_authorities: Goodes v East Sussex County Council [2000] 1 WLR 1356
Haydon v Kent County Council [1978] 1 QB 343

confidence.notes: Extensive review of highway maintenance authorities with clear unanimous outcome.

notes: Post-trial costs judgment in radio attendance patent action; issue-based percentage apportionment under CPR 44.3.

enrichment.short_title: DfES v Frontline: patent trial costs apportionment
key_facts: Following a June 2004 judgment, claims 1 and 2 of the Bromcom patent were invalid for lack of inventive step over Kingshurst but claim 7 was valid.
Neither party sought leave to appeal; dispute centred on costs apportionment across multiple validity issues at a two-week trial.
The claimant succeeded on Kingshurst but failed on SIMS, EARS intervening use, and documentary prior art.
The defendant performed a SIMS network traffic experiment found irrelevant and pursued subsidiary claims 3 to 6 until late concession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Argument on terms of order and issue-based costs following validity judgment in patent revocation action.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant ordered to pay defendant 8% of defendant's reasonable costs, subject to adjustments for interlocutory applications and late concession on claims 3 to 6; no order as to costs of the costs hearing.
enrichment.ratio: In partially successful patent proceedings, costs should be apportioned issue by issue by reference to trial time; a successful party on invalidity does not generally recover costs of failed validity attacks unless tied to successful ones; in exceptional cases an unsuccessful party may recover costs on particular issues without proof of unreasonable conduct.
legal_issues: Principles for issue-based costs apportionment under CPR 44.3
Apportionment between Kingshurst, SIMS, SYMBOL, EARS and common general knowledge issues
Reserved costs of evidential and experimental applications
Whether second expert Mr Wright's costs should be disallowed

Summit Property Ltd v Pitmans [2001] EWCA Civ 2020
Phonographic Performance Ltd v AIE Rediffusion Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 1507
Johnson Estates v Secretary of State for the Environment [2001] EWCA Civ 6535

notes: Appeal on inventorship of magnetic insect-trap patents; claimants failed to displace named inventors under section 7(4).

enrichment.short_title: IDA v Southampton: joint inventorship of magnetic insect traps
key_facts: Dispute over ownership of patent applications for insect traps using fine magnetic powder instead of electrostatic powder.
Mr Metcalfe suggested magnetic powder after reading a Times article about Professor Howse's electrostatic trap; confidential samples were supplied.
The Divisional Director held Metcalfe and Lax were sole inventors and removed Howse and Ashby, but the claimants had earlier acknowledged shared inventorship.
On appeal, defendants restricted their case to seeking reinstatement as joint inventors only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Comptroller's entitlement decision transferring patent applications entirely to claimants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; Professor Howse and Dr Ashby reinstated as joint inventors with Metcalfe and Lax because claimants failed to prove they contributed nothing to the inventive concepts.
enrichment.ratio: An inventor under section 7(3) is the person responsible for the inventive concept, not merely one who contributes enabling data; removing named inventors requires overcoming the section 7(4) presumption by proving they made no substantive contribution; Metcalfe's initial idea concerned the banana-skin trap effect, while Howse understood magnetic adhesion to insect cuticles enabling broader applications.
legal_issues: Who devised the pest/particle and particle-anchoring inventive concepts
Distinction between devising an invention and providing enabling disclosure
Onus on claimants to remove named inventors under section 7(4)
Whether defendants' all-or-nothing defence precluded joint inventorship finding
linked_authorities: Henry Brothers (Magherafelt) Ltd v Ministry of Defence [1997] RPC 693
Markham Corporation v Zipher Ltd (No 1) [2004] RPC 10
Collag Corp v Merck & Co Inc [2003] FSR 216

confidence.notes: Detailed inventorship analysis with clear limited relief on appeal. Factual findings of Divisional Director largely accepted.

notes: Mandatory lifer parole appeal; Parole Board held to have inherent power to appoint special advocate for sensitive material.

enrichment.short_title: Roberts v Parole Board: special advocate procedure
key_facts: Harry Roberts, convicted of murdering three police officers in 1966, faced recall review after alleged drug dealing and contraband in open prison.
Sensitive material was withheld from Roberts and his solicitors; Nicholas Blake QC was appointed as special advocate.
Sir Richard Tucker found genuine risk to source safety if full disclosure were made to Roberts or his representatives.
Roberts challenged whether the Parole Board had power to adopt the SIAC-style special advocate procedure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from administrative court upholding Parole Board use of special advocate in mandatory life prisoner release review.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Parole Board has inherent power under section 32 to adopt special advocate procedure in exceptional cases to balance public protection, prisoner fairness, and source safety.
enrichment.ratio: As a statutory court performing its protective role, the Parole Board may withhold sensitive evidence where disclosure poses real risk to sources and mitigate unfairness by appointing a special advocate; the procedure is not confined to national security and must remain exceptional; Article 5(4) permits proportionate qualification if substantial fairness is preserved.
legal_issues: Whether Parole Board has vires to appoint a special advocate for mandatory lifers
Compatibility with Article 5(4) and Article 6
Whether special advocate use is limited to national security cases
Whether 1997 Rules exhaust permissible departures from equality of arms
linked_authorities: Secretary of State v Rehman [2003] 1 AC 153

confidence.notes: Important procedural principle clearly decided. Merits of non-disclosure in Roberts' case not pursued on appeal.

notes: EPO multi-dose preservative patent revoked; combination of benzalkonium chloride with proteins not obvious to try.

enrichment.short_title: Sandoz v Roche: EPO preservative combination patent
key_facts: Revocation action against European Patent (UK) 0,607,156 on preserved multi-dose injectable erythropoietin formulations.
Roche sought to maintain amended claims limited to combinations of chlorobutanol, benzyl alcohol and benzalkonium chloride with EPO.
Claimant argued obviousness over common general knowledge, Konings, and Denyer/Boehm/Stock prior art.
No recombinant protein multi-dose formulation in 1991 used preservative combinations; benzalkonium chloride was recorded as incompatible with proteins.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on validity of amended patent claims after agreed postponement of amendment discretion issues.
enrichment.outcome: Patent revoked; amended combination claims lacked inventive step over common general knowledge and prior art did not make testing the combinations obvious.
enrichment.ratio: A skilled protein formulation team would conservatively select preservatives previously used with recombinant proteins; known synergies in general parenteral microbiology would not override established reservations about benzalkonium chloride and chlorobutanol with proteins; obvious-to-try requires a real prospect of valuable results, not mere experimentation.
legal_issues: Obviousness of combining specified preservatives in EPO multi-dose parenterals
Identity and common general knowledge of the skilled person/team
Effect of Konings shopping-list disclosure
Whether Denyer/Boehm synergy data made protein combinations obvious
linked_authorities: Windsurfing International Inc v Tabur Marine [1985] RPC 59
Rockwater Ltd v Technip France SA [2004] EWCA Civ 381

notes: Permission to appeal refused; E and R mistake-of-fact ground not open where IAT did not entertain credibility issue.

enrichment.short_title: Mazrae v SSHD: asylum credibility and E v SSHD
key_facts: Iranian Arab asylum seeker claimed persecution linked to university arson allegation and National Movement Alliance activity.
Adjudicator found applicant not credible and rejected expert report conclusions in that light.
Immigration Appeal Tribunal granted permission only on illegal departure ground, not credibility, and refused to revive the first ground.
Dr Browell's later report noted missing testicle and leg scarring possibly consistent with alleged beatings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from IAT dismissal of asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; tribunal was entitled not to consider adjudicator's credibility approach where that ground was not before it; E v SSHD mistake-of-fact principle could not reopen the case.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission to appeal to the IAT was granted only on the illegal departure ground, the court will not entertain a challenge to the adjudicator's credibility findings on renewed permission; new post-adjudication medical evidence does not justify restarting the asylum process in the Court of Appeal.
legal_issues: Whether IAT should have entertained credibility ground on E v SSHD principles
Adequacy of adjudicator's treatment of expert and medical evidence
Admissibility of new evidence on renewed permission application
Procedural fairness in asylum appeals
linked_authorities: E v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 49
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 49

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome clear though Sedley LJ expressed substantial doubts about adjudicator's credibility reasoning.

notes: Advance fee fraud convictions upheld; jury foreman's post-verdict note to prosecutor did not show bias.

enrichment.short_title: R v Alexander: advance fee fraud and jury bias
key_facts: Alexander, Andrews and Steen convicted after a five-and-a-half-month trial of conspiracy to defraud through an advance fee loan scheme.
Applicants paid reading, administration and due diligence fees but loans required unobtainable collateral bonds.
Eleven days after verdict the jury forewoman emailed and wrote to leading prosecution counsel inviting social contact and sending champagne.
Alexander and Steen appealed on alleged jury bias; Steen also sought leave to appeal his six-year sentence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction on jury bias ground and application for leave to appeal against sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed; Medicaments test not satisfied; no real possibility of jury bias; leave to appeal sentence refused.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Porter v Magill/Medicaments, post-verdict social communications from a juror to prosecuting counsel do not, without more, show real possibility of bias where the jury took their oath seriously, verdicts were unanimous and supported by strong evidence; advance fee fraud did not require proof that lies were told provided defendants knew applicants could not meet bond conditions.
legal_issues: Whether jury foreman's communications showed real possibility of bias
Admissibility of juror communications after verdict under Mirza principles
Whether Alexander's case should have been stopped for no case to answer
Whether six-year sentence on Steen was manifestly excessive

confidence.notes: Bias ground carefully analysed against established CA authorities. Underlying fraud scheme and verdict safety clearly explained.

notes: Tobacco smuggling appeal dismissed; 17 April letter was restoration request not Schedule 3 condemnation claim.

enrichment.short_title: Gascoyne v Customs: Schedule 3 notice construction
key_facts: Mr Gascoyne was stopped at Dover with 10,000 cigarettes and 32 kg of rolling tobacco in a Land Rover, far above guideline limits.
Goods and vehicle were seized; he claimed all tobacco was for personal use.
On 17 April 2001 he wrote requesting return of vehicle and goods and stating goods were for personal use not resale.
Customs treated the letter as a section 152 restoration request, not a Schedule 3 condemnation claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from High Court on whether April letter was a paragraph 3 Schedule 3 notice requiring condemnation proceedings and related Gora jurisdiction issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; letter construed in context of seizure notices as restoration request not condemnation claim; tribunal findings that Gascoyne was a commercial smuggler upheld on merits.
enrichment.ratio: A letter must be read as a whole in the context of Customs seizure notices distinguishing restoration from condemnation; a layman's sentence asserting own use does not necessarily constitute a Schedule 3 paragraph 3 claim where the overall tone seeks discretionary restoration; Gora obiter on deemed condemnation does not require a different construction outcome here.
legal_issues: Whether 17 April letter was a notice of claim under Schedule 3 paragraph 3 CEMA
Effect of Gora on tribunal jurisdiction to revisit lawfulness of seizure
Whether condemnation proceedings remained available in the High Court after delay
Whether goods imported for own use or commercial purpose
linked_authorities: Lindsay v Customs and Excise Commissioners [2002] 1 WLR 1766
Gora v Customs and Excise Commissioners [2004] QB 93
Mannai Investment Co v Eagle Star [1997] AC 767
Customs and Excise Commissioners v Newbury [2003] 1 WLR

confidence.notes: Construction point clearly decided though court also discussed Gora obiter and Convention implications at length.
